title: Natural Selection: Camouflage
objectives: Model how predation changes trait frequencies over generations (APES 2.5, 2.6)
Explain natural selection using data, including the role of mutation
Connect environmental change to evolution in real populations

steps.title: Briefing

npcLines: Some beetles are green, some are brown, and birds love to eat them. Which color survives depends on the ground they live on.
The tray on the middle bench lets us watch many generations in a few seconds. Start with bare soil.
how: Follow the yellow arrow and the compass at the top of the screen.
Walk with W A S D or the arrow keys. On an iPad, drag the joystick in the bottom-left corner.
When you are close, a button appears at the bottom of the screen. Press E or tap the button.
Read each line, then press Continue.

intro: Natural selection happens when individuals with certain inherited traits survive and reproduce more than others. Over many generations, those traits become more common.
In this model, birds hunt beetles. Beetles that blend in with the ground are harder for birds to see.
vocab: One round of parents producing offspring.
A trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.

steps.title: Bare soil

sequence.instruction: Set the ground to Bare soil, start at 50% green, and run at least 10 generations.

feedback.incorrect: Choose Bare soil and at least 10 generations.

how: Walk to the natural selection station (the middle bench) and step onto its glowing ring. The experiment panel opens.
On an iPad or phone the panel slides up from the bottom. Close it with ✕ when you are done.
Set 'Starting % green' to 50% and 'Generations' to 10 or more.
Press '▶ Run selection' and watch the graph.

question.prompt: In your bare-soil run, what percentage of beetles were BROWN in the final generation?
help: Find your Bare soil run in the 'Your runs' table.
Read the number in its 'Final brown' column.

feedback.correct: Correct, read straight from your data.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the 'Final brown' column for your bare-soil run.

question.prompt: Why did brown beetles become more common on bare soil?

options.label: Brown beetles blended in, so birds ate fewer of them and they produced more offspring
Green beetles changed their color to brown to survive
It was pure chance; color doesn't matter

feedback.correct: That's natural selection: the environment favored a trait that already existed.
feedback.incorrect: Individuals don't change their own color. Think about which beetles the birds could see.

steps.intro: Start with half green and half brown beetles on bare soil. Predict first: which color will the birds catch more often?

steps.title: Change the environment

sequence.instruction: Now set the ground to Grassland and run at least 10 generations.

feedback.correct: Run recorded: same beetles, different environment, opposite result.

how: At the natural selection station, choose Grassland under 'Habitat ground'.
Keep 'Generations' at 10 or more and press '▶ Run selection'.

question.prompt: If the mutation rate were set to 0%, what would happen in a population that is already 100% brown when it moves onto grass?

options.label: It could not become green, because there is no green variation left to select
The beetles would turn green within a few generations
Exactly the same as with mutation

sequence.hint: Try it: start at 0% green with 0% mutation on Grassland.

feedback.correct: Right. Selection can only act on variation that exists; mutation supplies new variation.
feedback.incorrect: Natural selection needs variation to act on. Test it in the tray.

question.prompt: Snowshoe hares turn white in winter to match snow. Climate change is shortening snowy seasons. Using what your beetle runs showed, predict what could happen to hare populations and explain why.
help: When there is no snow, which hares are easy for predators to see?
Use your beetle runs as evidence: what happened to the beetle color that didn't match the ground?
Predict what could happen to the hare population over many generations, and explain why variation matters (some hares may change color at different times).

steps.intro: Same beetles, new environment. When the environment changes, the trait that helps survival can change too.
vocab: A random change in DNA that can create a new trait.
Something in the environment (like predators) that affects which individuals survive.
